demeclocycline.text: Demeclocycline appears in de-puffing discussions because it makes the kidneys pass more free water, so some users speculate it could reduce water retention in the face. Its aquaretic effect has been studied in SIADH, and its use for facial puffiness is untested.

theobromine.text: Theobromine, the main xanthine in cocoa, is mentioned by users as a mild diuretic that might trim water weight and morning puffiness. Its diuretic effect is described in reference works, while its use for de-puffing the face has not been studied.

theophylline.text: Theophylline was first used as a diuretic in 1902, and some de-puffing discussions cite that history as a reason to consider it for water retention in the face. It is studied and prescribed for asthma and COPD; its use for puffiness is untested.

glycopyrrolate-oral.text: Oral glycopyrrolate is used off-label for excessive sweating, and some users take it to keep skin and clothing dry and look more composed. Its use for sweating is documented clinically, while evidence for appearance-specific use is limited.

glycopyrronium-tosylate-qbrexza.text: Qbrexza is a once-daily underarm wipe used to cut heavy underarm sweating, so users keep clothes free of sweat marks and feel more at ease in social settings. It is FDA-approved for axillary hyperhidrosis and supported by phase 3 trials.

propantheline.text: Propantheline is an older anticholinergic tablet that dermatology references list for excessive sweating, and users interested in staying dry and presentable look to it for that purpose. Sweat-specific trials were not found, so evidence for this use rests on reference listings.

aluminum-chloride-hexahydrate-drysol.text: Prescription-strength aluminium chloride is used on underarms, and sometimes hands and feet, to keep skin dry and clothes free of sweat marks. Dermatology sources describe it as a first-line treatment for hyperhidrosis, and reduced sweat is visible in use.

sofpironium-bromide-sofdra.text: Sofpironium bromide is a prescription underarm gel approved in Japan (2020) and the US (2024) for heavy sweating, taken up by people who want dry underarms and no sweat marks on clothing. It is an approved sweat treatment rather than a general appearance product.

zilpaterol-zilmax.text: Zilpaterol is a cattle feed additive that raises lean muscle in beef animals, and its link to looksmaxxing is the beta-agonist class that bodybuilders associate with leanness. No human studies exist and no documented human appearance use appears in the sources.

ractopamine-paylean.text: Ractopamine is a livestock feed additive that promotes lean muscle, and it surfaces in physique discussions as a beta-agonist relative of fat-loss drugs. No human appearance use is documented; it is mostly known in anti-doping contexts.

albuterol-salbutamol.text: Albuterol is an asthma rescue inhaler that some bodybuilders use for fat loss and muscle retention during cuts. Evidence for that use is scattered anecdote plus small lean-mass studies of oral dosing; its studied purpose is bronchospasm.

terbutaline.text: Terbutaline is a prescription asthma beta-2 agonist that physique forums group with albuterol and clenbuterol as a possible aid to leanness. It is studied for bronchospasm, and appearance trials do not exist.

rimonabant-acomplia.text: Rimonabant was a prescription weight-loss pill that blocks the CB1 receptor to cut appetite, and it is discussed as a past example of pharmaceutical fat loss. Trials showed weight loss; it was withdrawn in 2008 over mood effects.

lorcaserin-belviq.text: Lorcaserin (Belviq) was an FDA-approved prescription weight-loss pill that curbed appetite through serotonin 5-HT2C receptors. Trials showed modest weight loss compared with placebo, and it was withdrawn in 2020 over a cancer signal.

fenfluramine-phentermine-fen-phen.text: Fen-phen was a 1990s prescription pairing of two appetite suppressants, taken for weight loss and now cited as a historical diet-drug example. It produced weight loss in its era and was withdrawn in 1997 after heart valve problems.

dexfenfluramine-redux.text: Dexfenfluramine (Redux) was a 1990s prescription serotonin-acting diet pill for obesity, and appears in discussions of past weight-loss drugs. It was studied for appetite and weight reduction, and was pulled in 1997 over heart-valve and lung-pressure harms.

phenylpropanolamine.text: Phenylpropanolamine was a decongestant and over-the-counter diet-pill stimulant, once common in weight-loss products and cited as a historical appetite suppressant. It was removed from the market in the early 2000s after a hemorrhagic stroke link.

obetrol-amphetamine-salts.text: Obetrol was a 1950s and 1960s prescription diet pill of amphetamine and methamphetamine salts marketed for obesity, and is cited as the ancestor of Adderall. It is of historical interest in diet-pill discussions.

cetilistat.text: Cetilistat is an orlistat-style lipase inhibitor, taken so some dietary fat passes through unabsorbed and weight comes down. It has phase 2 data for weight loss and is available mainly in Japan.

plenity-gelesis100.text: Plenity is a swallowed hydrogel capsule taken before meals to promote fullness, used for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity. It is cleared as a device and trials show modest weight loss.

hu6.text: HU6 is an investigational slow-release prodrug of DNP, a fat-burning mitochondrial uncoupler, and is followed by people interested in a more controlled version of DNP-style fat loss. It is in phase 2 trials and is not available as a product.

ubt251.text: UBT251 is an investigational once-weekly triple agonist, licensed to Novo Nordisk, that people follow as a next-generation weight-loss peptide after semaglutide and tirzepatide. Phase 2 data exist, and it is not an approved or prescribable drug.

benzphetamine.text: Benzphetamine is a prescription amphetamine-type appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment, and appears in discussions of older weight-loss drugs. It is a Schedule III medication aimed at weight reduction, not a cosmetic drug.

phendimetrazine.text: Phendimetrazine is an older prescription stimulant appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment, and is mentioned alongside similar diet drugs. It is a controlled medication for weight reduction, not a cosmetic drug.

diethylpropion.text: Diethylpropion is an older prescription appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment, and it is discussed with other diet drugs. It is Schedule IV in the US, and the EU has recommended its withdrawal.

pioglitazone.text: Pioglitazone is a type 2 diabetes drug known to raise subcutaneous fat, which is why appearance discussions bring it up in connection with body-fat distribution. Appearance-related claims about it are untested in humans.

anamorelin.text: Anamorelin is an investigational oral ghrelin-receptor drug studied for cancer cachexia, and muscle-focused users follow it because it raised lean mass in trials. Those trials were in cancer patients, and appearance-use data are absent.

macimorelin.text: Macimorelin is an oral ghrelin-receptor agonist that releases growth hormone, and GH-minded users note it as a secretagogue. It is approved only as a one-time diagnostic test for adult GH deficiency, with no data on appearance.

capromorelin.text: Capromorelin is an oral ghrelin agonist sold as a pet appetite stimulant, and it draws interest as a growth hormone secretagogue. A human older-adult trial showed a modest lean-mass change and was not pursued.

relamorelin.text: Relamorelin is an injected ghrelin analogue studied for diabetic gastroparesis, and some people group it with ghrelin-pathway muscle and appetite compounds. Phase 3 trials were terminated and appearance data do not exist.
